clue.text: Quality of ladies very ordinary

blocks.note: the ladies is a women's toilet, and bog is British slang for a toilet
a standard is a level of quality

explanation.surface: A remark about the quality of some ladies, or a ladies' toilet, being nothing special.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives quality first, but the answer puts the ladies first: 'Quality of ladies' is read as ladies' quality. Bog is British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Bog-standard is informal British for basic and unremarkable, with nothing extra or special about it.

clue.text: Neurologist throws out crisp banalities

indicators.note: things thrown out land scattered in a new order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fifteen letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A neurologist sharply dismisses a colleague's dull, obvious remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throws out' reads as rejecting the banalities, but it is the signal to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: A neurologist is a doctor who specialises in disorders of the brain and nervous system.

clue.text: Exhilaration of oxygen after sudden wind

blocks.note: a gust is a brief rush of wind
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: The thrill of breathing fresh air after a sudden blast of wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the oxygen symbol behind the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusto is hearty enjoyment or zest, close in sense to exhilaration.

clue.text: It's awfully hard to hide a navy stain

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the letters come out jumbled
to hide something is to put it inside cover, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
taken as written
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A warning that some naval paint or uniform is hard to keep clean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' applies to the apostrophe word and the hard abbreviation together; the navy pair then sits inside that jumble just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarnish is to discolour or sully, so as a verb it means to stain.

clue.text: Figure almost dead? A long time left

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: numb means without feeling, as in a dead limb
an era is a long period
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone who has been nearly dead for ages, perhaps a ghost of a figure left behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A numeral is a written figure or digit standing for a number.

clue.text: Like member of family to be a support

blocks.note: as means in the manner of, like
a sister is a female sibling

explanation.surface: Advice to support someone the way a sibling would.
explanation.definitionFit: An assister is a helper, someone who gives backing or help, which is what a support is.

clue.text: Curtail activities, but complete self-portrait as a Devil?

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for cutting back on spending or ambition
second meaning, read literally: sketch your own horns onto a picture of yourself

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom comes from a snail pulling in its horns; the second reading takes 'draw' as making a picture, so you finish a Devil self-portrait by adding horns.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw in one's horns is an idiom meaning to retreat or economise, to scale back what one is doing.

clue.text: Such a forced wedding heartless for Japanese ruler

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter of the word is taken out

blocks.note: a shotgun wedding is one forced on a couple, traditionally by a pregnancy

explanation.surface: A forced marriage lacking love, arranged for a Japanese ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: The seven-letter word loses its middle letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: A shogun was a hereditary military dictator who ruled Japan in place of the emperor.

clue.text: After a time children's author becoming vulgar

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
the Rev W. Awdry wrote the Thomas the Tank Engine books

explanation.surface: A children's writer whose work turned crude over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After a time' puts the author behind T. Awdry was the clergyman who created Thomas the Tank Engine.
explanation.definitionFit: Tawdry means showy but cheap and tasteless, a close synonym of vulgar.

clue.text: He roars uncontrollably, becoming this?

indicators.note: without control the letters run wild and land in another order

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man shouting without restraint ends up with a rough voice.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: roaring wildly makes your voice rougher.
explanation.definitionFit: Roaring strains the vocal cords, so a shouter's voice becomes more husky and rasping.

clue.text: I give black marks for going on the lash

definitions.text: I give black marks for going on the lash

blocks.clueFragment: I give black marks for going on the lash
blocks.note: surface reading: a disapproving judge marking down someone who goes out drinking or a flogging
setter's reading: a lash is an eyelash, and a cosmetic darkens eyelashes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going on the lash' is British slang for a night of heavy drinking, and black marks sound like demerits; really the lash is an eyelash and the marks are make-up.
explanation.definitionFit: This cosmetic is brushed onto eyelashes to darken and thicken them, leaving black colour there.

clue.text: Roughly ignore old punter

indicators.note: roughly means not precisely, so the letters are only loosely kept and rearranged

blocks.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to brush off an elderly gambler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punter' suggests a gambler or customer, but here it is someone who propels a boat with a pole.
explanation.definitionFit: A gondolier propels a Venetian boat with a pole, so he is one who punts in the boating sense.

clue.text: Thrown, Vulcan takes refuge in hut

indicators.note: taking refuge in a place means going inside it for shelter

blocks.note: a shed is a simple hut
Vulcan is the setter, who refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: The setter, rattled, hides away in a hut.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym stands for the first person. The pronoun goes inside the hut: SH(I)ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Shied is a past tense of shy, meaning flung or tossed, so it equals thrown.

clue.text: Exercise unavailable? Definitely not

blocks.note: no as in none on offer, as in 'no exercise'
PE is physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether a workout is possible, and being flatly refused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exercise unavailable' is read as 'no PE', putting the negative first.
explanation.definitionFit: Nope is an informal emphatic no, a firm refusal.

clue.text: Cyclone had disturbed rock

indicators.note: disturbed things are thrown out of their settled order

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A storm has shaken up the landscape, moving the stones around.
explanation.definitionFit: Chalcedony is a microcrystalline quartz mineral, a kind of rock used for gems such as agate and onyx.

clue.text: Charge through the gate

blocks.note: surface reading: rush forward and burst through a gateway
setter's reading: a charge is a price, and the gate is the turnstile at a sports ground, so this is the price paid to get in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' first reads as a stampede; it is really a fee. At British sports grounds 'the gate' also means the paying attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the sum paid for admission to an event or venue, collected at the entrance.

clue.text: I'll be round in a minute

definitions.text: I'll be round in a minute

blocks.clueFragment: I'll be round in a minute
blocks.note: surface reading: someone promising to call on you shortly
setter's reading: a pointer on a clock sweeps once around the dial every sixty seconds

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase sounds like a friend about to drop by; read literally it describes a clock pointer making one full circuit per minute.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the clock hand that marks seconds, completing a full revolution of the dial each minute.

clue.text: Rather watery prune mole eats

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: a mole is a spy planted inside an organisation
to prune is to lop or cut back

explanation.surface: A gardener's note on a mole nibbling a prune in a damp garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prune' looks like the dried plum, but it is the verb to cut back. The spy surrounds it: S(LOP)PY.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloppy food or ground is wet and runny, containing too much liquid.

clue.text: Henry, shoe repairer not opening for one with a limp

indicators.note: without its opening means the first letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
a cobbler mends shoes

explanation.surface: A man called Henry and a cobbler who isn't open for business, serving someone who walks with difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Henry' looks like a man's name; it is the physics unit. Fittingly, a limping customer needs a shoe repairer.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobble is to walk awkwardly or lamely, so a hobbler is a person who limps.

clue.text: A different satellite? It's the same one each time

definitions.text: A different satellite? It's the same one each time

blocks.note: surface reading: a fresh body orbiting the earth

blocks.clueFragment: It's the same one each time
blocks.note: setter's reading: the phase of our one natural satellite that begins each lunar month, which looks like a fresh one but never is

explanation.walkthrough: The question invites a second, replacement moon; the answer is a phase of the one we already have, which recurs every month.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the lunar phase when the moon is dark and begins its cycle again, so it is called fresh though it is the same body.

clue.text: I went first, coming round to shop

indicators.note: coming round means turning about, so the letters are read back to front

blocks.note: taken as written
to lead is to go first; led is its past tense

explanation.surface: Someone describing walking ahead, then turning to visit a store.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of 'I went first', I LED, is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: A deli, short for delicatessen, is a shop selling cooked meats, cheeses and prepared foods.

clue.text: The aim of camping?

blocks.note: first meaning: purpose or goal
second meaning, split in two: when camping you are inside canvas

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading: the answer splits into IN TENT, which is where a camper is.
explanation.definitionFit: Intent is a noun for purpose or intention, the thing one is aiming at.

clue.text: A single short song going out to listeners

indicators.note: short means cut down, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a single thing is one
an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A radio presenter playing one brief song for the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' suggests a pop record, which suits the radio scene, but it simply means one.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme that is on air is being broadcast, transmitted to people listening at that moment.

clue.text: This ahead for person taking over? Unlikely

definitions.text: This ahead for person taking over? Unlikely

blocks.clueFragment: This ahead for person taking over?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone taking over a business or office, with something lying ahead of them

blocks.clueFragment: ahead for person taking over? Unlikely
blocks.note: setter's reading: 'ahead' is 'a head', and the person taking an over in cricket is the one delivering the ball; such a player would hardly wear headgear named after himself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ahead' splits into 'a head', and 'taking over' is the cricket sense: an over is a set of six balls, delivered by one player. That player wearing this formal hat would be odd, hence 'Unlikely'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the hard round felt hat once worn by City gents, sharing its name with the cricket player who delivers an over.

clue.text: Does she check and improve husband?

blocks.note: editing means checking and correcting a text
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A question about whether a wife reviews and improves her husband's work or manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is the definition: the answer is a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith is a female first name, so it fits the pronoun standing for a woman.

clue.text: Hurting Dad almost completely

indicators.note: almost means not quite the whole, so the phrase loses its final letter

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
in full means completely, with nothing left out

explanation.surface: A child complaining that their father has hurt them nearly as much as possible.
explanation.definitionFit: Painful as an adjective means causing pain, as a hurting injury does.

clue.text: Character is a moronic sort

indicators.note: to sort things is to put them into a different arrangement

blocks.note: the seven letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict that some person is a stupid type.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person, which suits the insult, but it means a letter of an alphabet; 'sort' looks like a noun meaning type but works as the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Omicron is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, and a letter is a character.

clue.text: They were cut out for war

definitions.text: They were cut out for war

blocks.clueFragment: They were cut out for war
blocks.note: surface reading: soldiers who were naturally suited to fighting
setter's reading: literally dug out of the ground to serve in the First World War

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut out for' means born to do; read literally, these were excavated for the Great War, where the Western Front was fought from dugout lines.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the network of dug defensive ditches on the Western Front in the First World War.
